question.html:
Question 51
?

To measure the success of an amusement park, Ed uses the following three functions that model the daily number of visitors to the park t minutes after the park is opened to the public.

  • N(t) - the number of people inside the park

  • E(t) - the rate at which people enter the park

  • L(t) - the rate at which people leave the park

What is the relationship between the functions above?

a
N′(t)=E(t)−L(t)
b
N′(t)=E(t)+L(t)
c
N(t)=E(t)+L(t)
d
N(t)=E(t)−L(t)
e
N′(t)=E(t)⋅L(t)
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function N(t) gives the number of people inside the park t minutes after opening. Then, N′(t)=dN(t)dt=Change in NChange in t. Thus, N′(t) gives the rate at which the number of people inside the park changes t minutes after opening.

In addition, we can compute the rate of change of the number of people inside the park at time t by finding the difference between the entry and exit rates at time t. That is, N′(t)=E(t)−L(t).

last_observation.worked_solution:
The function $N(t)$ gives the number of people inside the park $t$ minutes after opening. Then,

$$
{N}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}N(t)}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{Change in }N}{\text{Change in }t}.
$$

Thus, ${N}^{′}(t)$ gives the rate at which the number of people inside the park changes $t$ minutes after opening.

In addition, we can compute the rate of change of the number of people inside the park at time $t$ by finding the difference between the entry and exit rates at time $t.$ That is,

$$
{N}^{′}(t)=E(t)-L(t).
$$

question.html:
Question 51
?

To measure the success of an amusement park, Ed uses the following three functions that model the daily number of visitors to the park t minutes after the park is opened to the public.

  • N(t) - the number of people inside the park

  • E(t) - the rate at which people enter the park

  • L(t) - the rate at which people leave the park

What is the relationship between the functions above?

a
N′(t)=E(t)−L(t)
b
N′(t)=E(t)+L(t)
c
N(t)=E(t)+L(t)
d
N(t)=E(t)−L(t)
e
N′(t)=E(t)⋅L(t)
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function N(t) gives the number of people inside the park t minutes after opening. Then, N′(t)=dN(t)dt=Change in NChange in t. Thus, N′(t) gives the rate at which the number of people inside the park changes t minutes after opening.

In addition, we can compute the rate of change of the number of people inside the park at time t by finding the difference between the entry and exit rates at time t. That is, N′(t)=E(t)−L(t).

solution.reasoning: The rate of change of the number inside equals the entry rate minus the departure rate: N′(t)=E(t)−L(t), option a. Both sides have units of people per minute. No Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence is captured.

feedback.html:
Question 51
?

To measure the success of an amusement park, Ed uses the following three functions that model the daily number of visitors to the park t minutes after the park is opened to the public.

  • N(t) - the number of people inside the park

  • E(t) - the rate at which people enter the park

  • L(t) - the rate at which people leave the park

What is the relationship between the functions above?

a
N′(t)=E(t)−L(t)
b
N′(t)=E(t)+L(t)
c
N(t)=E(t)+L(t)
d
N(t)=E(t)−L(t)
e
N′(t)=E(t)⋅L(t)
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function N(t) gives the number of people inside the park t minutes after opening. Then, N′(t)=dN(t)dt=Change in NChange in t. Thus, N′(t) gives the rate at which the number of people inside the park changes t minutes after opening.

In addition, we can compute the rate of change of the number of people inside the park at time t by finding the difference between the entry and exit rates at time t. That is, N′(t)=E(t)−L(t).

question.name: Question 52
question.problem: Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ when $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt[5]{{x}^{2}}}.$
question.worked_solution:
Writing the radical as a rational exponent, we have

$$
y=\frac{1}{\sqrt[5]{{x}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{{x}^{2/5}}={x}^{-2/5}
$$

Applying the power rule with $n=-\frac{2}{5},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-2/5}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}{x}^{-2/5-1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}{x}^{-7/5} \\  & =-\frac{2}{5{x}^{7/5}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{5\sqrt[5]{{x}^{7}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 52
?

Find dydx when y=1x25.

a
−25x27
b
52x75
c
75x25
d
−25x75
e
−25x57
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing the radical as a rational exponent, we have

y=1x25=1x2/5=x−2/5

Applying the power rule with n=−25, we get

dydx=ddx(x−2/5)=−25x−2/5−1=−25x−7/5=−25x7/5=−25x75.

$$
y=\frac{1}{\sqrt[5]{{x}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{{x}^{2/5}}={x}^{-2/5}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-2/5}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}{x}^{-2/5-1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}{x}^{-7/5} \\  & =-\frac{2}{5{x}^{7/5}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{5\sqrt[5]{{x}^{7}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 52
?

Find dydx when y=1x25.

a
−25x27
b
52x75
c
75x25
d
−25x75
e
−25x57
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing the radical as a rational exponent, we have

y=1x25=1x2/5=x−2/5

Applying the power rule with n=−25, we get

dydx=ddx(x−2/5)=−25x−2/5−1=−25x−7/5=−25x7/5=−25x75.

solution.reasoning: Rewrite y=x^(−2/5). The power rule gives dy/dx=−(2/5)x^(−7/5)=−2/(5√[5](x⁷)), valid for x≠0. Thus option d is correct. No Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence is captured.

feedback.name: Question 52
feedback.problem: Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ when $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt[5]{{x}^{2}}}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Writing the radical as a rational exponent, we have

$$
y=\frac{1}{\sqrt[5]{{x}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{{x}^{2/5}}={x}^{-2/5}
$$

Applying the power rule with $n=-\frac{2}{5},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-2/5}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}{x}^{-2/5-1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}{x}^{-7/5} \\  & =-\frac{2}{5{x}^{7/5}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{5\sqrt[5]{{x}^{7}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 53
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14196632/assets/95c30eab094a24beb6976262167401efa973dbac12781c69d074eb14e12e2743.png)

Consider the picture above. Which of the following is a unit vector that is parallel to $m+n?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we have to find $m+n.$ According to the triangle law of addition, the resultant $m+n$ goes from the tail of $m$ to the head of $n:$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14196632/assets/87647211f77776c5f5f740c205fafb150eef1b9d3ebefb82df73a9fdcd953bdb.png)

In $△AHB$, we have $∠AHB={90}^{∘}$, $AH=0.5=\frac{1}{2}$ and $BH=2.$ So, the Pythagorean theorem gives

$$
\begin{aligned}|m+n| & =AB \\  & =\sqrt{A{H}^{2}+B{H}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+4} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{17}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the magnitude of $m+n$ is $\frac{\sqrt{17}}{2}.$ Consequently, the unit vector is

$$

12(m+n)

First, we have to find m+n. According to the triangle law of addition, the resultant m+n goes from the tail of m to the head of n:

In △AHB, we have ∠AHB=90∘, AH=0.5=12 and BH=2. So, the Pythagorean theorem gives

|m+n|=AB=AH2+BH2=(12)2+22=14+4=172.

Hence, the magnitude of m+n is 172. Consequently, the unit vector is u=1|m+n|⋅(m+n)=217(m+n).

Consider the picture above. Which of the following is a unit vector that is parallel to $m+n?$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we have to find $m+n.$ According to the triangle law of addition, the resultant $m+n$ goes from the tail of $m$ to the head of $n:$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14196632/assets/87647211f77776c5f5f740c205fafb150eef1b9d3ebefb82df73a9fdcd953bdb.png)

In $△AHB$, we have $∠AHB={90}^{∘}$, $AH=0.5=\frac{1}{2}$ and $BH=2.$ So, the Pythagorean theorem gives

$$
\begin{aligned}|m+n| & =AB \\  & =\sqrt{A{H}^{2}+B{H}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+4} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{17}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the magnitude of $m+n$ is $\frac{\sqrt{17}}{2}.$ Consequently, the unit vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{1}{|m+n|}\cdot (m+n) \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{17}}(m+n).\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Find where the tangent to the curve $y=6\sqrt{x}+5x-13$ at the point $(1,-2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
question.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=6\sqrt{x}+5x-13.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6\sqrt{x}+5x-13) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{x}^{1/2}+5x) \\  & =3{x}^{-1/2}+5\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=3(1)^{-1/2}+5=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-2) & =8(x-1) \\ y & =8x-8-2 \\ y & =8x-10.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 54
?

Find where the tangent to the curve y=6x+5x−13 at the point (1,−2) intersects the x-axis.

a
(0,−54)
b
(−54,0)
c
(5,0)
d
(54,0)
e
(4,0)
Don't Know
Submit
Skipped Question
EXPLANATION

Let f(x)=6x+5x−13. Let's first calculate the derivative:

f′(x)=ddx(6x+5x−13)=ddx(6x1/2+5x)=3x−1/2+5

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is m=f′(1)=3(1)−1/2+5=8.

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

y−y1=m(x−x1)y−(−2)=8(x−1)y=8x−8−2y=8x−10.

To find where the tangent line intercepts the x-axis, we set y=0 and solve:

0=8x−10x=54

Therefore, the point of intersection is (54,0).

feedback.problem: Find where the tangent to the curve $y=6\sqrt{x}+5x-13$ at the point $(1,-2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
feedback.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=6\sqrt{x}+5x-13.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6\sqrt{x}+5x-13) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{x}^{1/2}+5x) \\  & =3{x}^{-1/2}+5\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=3(1)^{-1/2}+5=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-2) & =8(x-1) \\ y & =8x-8-2 \\ y & =8x-10.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $y=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =8x-10 \\ x & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(\frac{5}{4},0).$

question.name: Question 56
question.problem: $\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt[4]{e})=$
question.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite $\sqrt[4]{e}$ as a power of $e$ (the base of the natural logarithm) as follows:

$$
\sqrt[4]{e}={e}^{1/4}
$$

Therefore, we have:

$$
\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt[4]{e})=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{1/4})
$$

The natural logarithm reverses the action of the exponent. The principle is:

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x})=x
$$

In our case, we have $x=\frac{1}{4}.$ Therefore:

$$
\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{1/4})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{8}
$$

Question 56

12ln⁡(e4)=

a
12
b
14
c
16
d
18
e
2
Don't Know

Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we rewrite e4 as a power of e (the base of the natural logarithm) as follows: e4=e1/4

Therefore, we have:

12ln⁡(e4)=12ln⁡(e1/4)

The natural logarithm reverses the action of the exponent. The principle is: ln⁡(ex)=x

In our case, we have x=14. Therefore: 12ln⁡(e1/4)=12⋅14=18

topic_match.reasoning: This tests evaluating a natural logarithm using ln(e^r)=r. Since the fourth root of e is e^(1/4), the expression equals (1/2)(1/4)=1/8. It matches The Natural Logarithm.

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite $\sqrt[4]{e}$ as a power of $e$ (the base of the natural logarithm) as follows:

$$
\sqrt[4]{e}={e}^{1/4}
$$

Therefore, we have:

$$
\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt[4]{e})=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{1/4})
$$

The natural logarithm reverses the action of the exponent. The principle is:

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x})=x
$$

In our case, we have $x=\frac{1}{4}.$ Therefore:

$$
\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{1/4})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{8}
$$

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14196632/assets/23f0dba237502bc7261fd8f28327beefd5872bb4b0f503930c488b2857fcef24.png)

Given that the point $A$ has coordinates $(-\sqrt{3},-1),$ calculate the angle $\theta .$
question.worked_solution:
We can form a triangle by creating a vertical line from $A$ to the $x$-axis. Let us call ${\theta }^{′}$ the acute angle that is formed with the $x$-axis such that ${\theta }^{′}+{180}^{∘}=\theta $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14196632/assets/d14f62179f831ebdc177eac7bd2899679864305d4104d4b61f304eb4fa9e133d.png)

Using the tangent ratio, we have

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡{\theta }^{′}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.
$$

Finally, using the inverse tangent, we get

$$
{\theta }^{′}=\operatorname{arctan}⁡\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}={30}^{∘}.
$$

Finally, using $\theta ={\theta }^{′}+{180}^{∘},$ we get $\theta ={30}^{∘}+{180}^{∘}={210}^{∘}.$

question.html:
Question 57
?

Given that the point A has coordinates (−3,−1), calculate the angle θ.

a
 220∘
b
 210∘
c
 190∘
d
 230∘
e
 200∘
Don't Know
Submit
Skipped Question
EXPLANATION

We can form a triangle by creating a vertical line from A to the x-axis. Let us call θ′ the acute angle that is formed with the x-axis such that θ′+180∘=θ

Using the tangent ratio, we have

tan⁡θ′=13=33.

Finally, using the inverse tangent, we get

θ′=arctan⁡33=30∘.

Finally, using θ=θ′+180∘, we get θ=30∘+180∘=210∘.

topic_match.reasoning: The question uses special trigonometric ratios to recover an angle from a point in quadrant III. The reference angle satisfies tan(α)=1/√3, giving α=30° and θ=180°+30°=210°. This best matches Further Extensions of the Special Trigonometric Ratios.
